There is a particular quiet that belongs only to early morning, before the world has remembered all its errands and arguments. It settles on rooftops and kitchen tables alike, softening edges that will sharpen later. I like to sit with it, coffee in hand, watching light move slowly across the floor as if the sun itself were learning the room for the first time. Nothing important happens in those minutes, and that is precisely their gift.

Memory works differently. It does not arrive in order. A song will open a door to a summer I thought forgotten, complete with sunscreen and traffic on an old road I no longer live near. A word, overheard on a bus, will return me to a conversation that ended years ago, and suddenly I am answering differently, braver, kinder, as if I could revise the past with better lines.

Perhaps that is why we keep returning to certain places, not because they are beautiful in any objective sense, but because they hold versions of ourselves we are reluctant to lose. A chipped mug. A park bench. The corner where we once waited, hoping for news that never came. These ordinary things become archives.

I do not believe life needs to be extraordinary to be worth noticing. Most days are made of small repetitions: opening a door, feeding a plant, laughing at something not particularly funny because we are tired and happy to be together. If you pay attention long enough, even repetition reveals change.
